intro: Written in 1912, the Second Sonata puts long melodies, a short scherzo and a tarantella finale into four movements. Listen for the accompaniment: changing the notes beneath a melody often changes its character more drastically than changing the melody itself.
question: How does the accompaniment change the character of a melody?

These excerpts compare the expanding phrase in the two outer sections, as described in Emilia Zanetti’s account at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. relations.label: An earlier melody returns in the finale
relations.basis: The finale recalls the first movement’s cantabile material. The measured pair crosses those movements and agrees with this cyclic recollection, documented at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: In the opening, the melody groups notes in pairs above an accompaniment divided into threes. Try following the two layers separately: they organise the same underlying pulse differently.
cues.evidence: Emilia Zanetti’s Santa Cecilia programme note describes the opening’s duple figure over triplet arpeggios. This is an opening-texture guide, not an attack-time claim. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A longer melodic breath
cues.text: In the first movement’s more restrained passages, follow the tune across the accompaniment’s smaller gestures. Contrast can lie in the length of the phrase, not only in how strongly the piano is played.
cues.evidence: Zanetti describes the lyrical second idea. The comparatively restrained region around 1:05–1:35 suggests its broad position, without a reviewed score alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Renewed activity after a close
cues.text: Across this stretch, a quiet passage gives way to renewed activity. Listen for whether earlier figures are repeated whole or broken into shorter units.
cues.evidence: Relative level and attack density rise around 1:55–2:10. The report supports a renewed active passage but does not itself identify the start of a development.

cues.title: The central build
cues.text: Through this part of the first movement, successive gestures gather weight over an extended span. Compare that growth with a single accented chord: accumulation depends on what follows as well as the initial attack.
cues.evidence: Relative level increases across approximately 2:35–3:15 before falling back around 3:30–3:35.

cues.title: Returning with another balance
cues.text: In the later part of the movement, compare familiar figures with their earlier accompaniments. The score’s recapitulation changes the opening material; recognising a return does not mean hearing an unchanged replay.
cues.evidence: Zanetti describes the altered, largely quiet recapitulation. Its location is estimated from score order and the recording’s changing texture around 3:42, not verified by ear.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Growing out of a sonatina
cues.text: The first movement developed from an earlier sonatina. The scherzo also reused earlier work, written for Lyadov’s class; the final two movements were added to complete the four-movement sonata in 1912.
cues.evidence: Zanetti’s programme note traces this construction through Prokofiev’s autobiography and Nestyev’s account. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html

cues.title: A closing surge
cues.text: Near the first movement’s close, the piano gathers force and then withdraws. Keep that compact ending distinct from the shorter, more sharply articulated movement that follows.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 5:20–5:35 and falls around 5:40–5:45, before a new active stretch. The movement boundary remains approximate.

cues.title: Short figures in the scherzo
cues.text: The scherzo compresses its argument into brief, accented gestures. Listen for the accompaniment’s recurring motion beneath them, rather than expecting the first movement’s long melodic spans.
cues.evidence: Both programme notes on the Flaminio page describe the scherzo’s short figures. Increased recorded activity around 5:50–6:15 supports this approximate movement placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The short movement gathers weight
cues.text: Across the later scherzo passage, quieter gestures give way to stronger, closely packed attacks. Compare their compact rhythm with the more widely spaced writing of the slow movement that follows.
cues.evidence: Relative level and attack density rise around 6:55–7:15, with a pronounced reduction near 7:30.

cues.title: Space in the Andante
cues.text: The slow movement sets a longer melody above recurring accompaniment. Listen for the line continuing across the decay of individual piano notes; sustaining a phrase is not the same as sustaining one note.
cues.evidence: Zanetti describes the Andante’s melody and rocking bass. Its approximate placement follows the quieter, sparsely articulated stretch after about 7:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A slow phrase expands
cues.text: Across this passage, the sound gains weight without matching the scherzo’s density of attacks. A longer phrase can grow stronger while leaving more space between its notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 8:00–8:45 while attack density remains lower than in the preceding scherzo’s busiest stretches.

cues.title: Between melody and bass
cues.text: Through the Andante, try listening between the highest melody and the lowest support. The score gives moving inner notes their own line; they need not function only as chord filling.
cues.evidence: Zanetti describes the Andante’s layered writing and chromatic inner line. The prompt does not claim to locate an individual entry. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Weight in the slow movement
cues.text: The slow movement reaches a substantial crest in this stretch. Compare its weight with the earlier fast writing: more force does not necessarily require more densely packed attacks.
cues.evidence: The recording’s highest five-second relative-level windows cluster around 10:35–10:45. Detected attacks are less frequent than in the scherzo’s busiest passages.

cues.title: Lyricism in retrospect
cues.text: In his 1941 autobiography, Prokofiev ranked the lyrical element in his music above the toccata-like element. That is a later account of his own priorities, not a contemporary programme for the Second Sonata.
cues.evidence: Simon Morrison’s Henle preface, p. IV, quotes and contextualises the 1941 autobiography. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: A tarantella finale
cues.text: The finale takes up a tarantella rhythm, with each main beat divided into three. Listen for continuous smaller motion replacing the Andante’s longer spans.
cues.evidence: Zanetti identifies the tarantella. The large rise in relative level around 11:45–11:55 suggests the movement’s approximate start, not a verified first-note time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The rush can be interrupted
cues.text: Through the finale, listen for withdrawals within the running activity. A quieter gap can redirect the argument without bringing the movement to an end.
cues.evidence: The report shows a marked fall in relative level around 13:10–13:25, followed by renewed activity near 13:30.

cues.title: Attacks crowd together again
cues.text: Across this stretch, the restart becomes busier and stronger. Follow a larger melodic contour through the quick notes rather than giving every attack equal emphasis.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks and relative level rise around 13:45–14:05. The suggested melodic grouping is not an automatic transcription.

cues.title: Publication before the premiere
cues.text: Jurgenson published the sonata in Moscow in 1913. Its first public performance followed in Moscow on 5 February 1914, two years after composition.
cues.evidence: The Flaminio work catalogue gives composition, first-edition and premiere dates. https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html

cues.title: Weight through the closing passage
cues.text: Across the close, the piano maintains substantial weight before its final decay. Listen beyond the last attacks without expecting an extended quiet section to follow them.
cues.evidence: Relative level remains comparatively steady around 15:45–16:05, then drops sharply by 16:15, when no further attacks are detected.

transitions.title: A full stop replaces the long argument
transitions.how: The first movement completes its D-minor argument rather than modulating through a connecting passage. The separate Scherzo starts a sharper kind of motion in A minor: short accented gestures strike against an insistent accompaniment. The piano’s bass and chords now supply a repeating rhythmic mechanism instead of supporting the preceding movement’s long phrases and triplet arpeggios. No melody is carried bodily across the boundary; the continuity lies in the instrument’s percussive attack, now compressed into a smaller form.
transitions.evidence: The approximate Scherzo boundary is 5:50. Analysis shows a first-movement closing rise at 5:30–5:35, withdrawal at 5:40–5:45 and renewed attacks at 5:50. The score supplies the separate movements, D-minor/A-minor relationship and Scherzo texture; the provisional relation already places a Scherzo excerpt at 5:48.5. No exact silence or first note is asserted.

transitions.title: The repeating mechanism becomes a rocking bass
transitions.how: The Scherzo’s clipped A-minor writing ends before the Andante establishes G♯ minor, a semitone lower. This is a new movement’s tonal placement, not a pivot-chord modulation. The busy accompaniment is replaced by a slower rocking bass, over which the right hand can sustain a longer melodic sentence. Low support and upper song are more widely separated in rhythmic scale; the piano’s decay between attacks becomes part of the phrase instead of a gap to be filled by another accent.
transitions.evidence: The Andante marker is approximately 7:34, between measured boundaries at 7:32 and 7:36. Relative level and attack density fall sharply after 7:25. The score supplies the G♯-minor slow movement; Zanetti describes its melody and rocking bass at https://www.flaminioonline.it/Guide/Prokofiev/Prokofiev-Sonata14.html. The analyser’s A♭-minor spelling is corroboration only.

transitions.title: The slow line breaks into a tarantella
transitions.how: The Andante withdraws before the finale re-establishes D minor and a fast 6/8 tarantella. Prokofiev does not smooth G♯ minor into the home key with an extended bridge: the new movement announces a different tonal and rhythmic footing. Repeated smaller notes replace the slow melody’s sustained spans, and bass and upper register take part in the new motor rhythm. The sonata’s earlier lyricism will return later in the finale, but it is not the material that makes this initial join.
transitions.evidence: The finale boundary is approximately 11:52, the strongest measured change. Level falls towards 11:45 then rises sharply by 11:50–11:55. The score supplies the D-minor Vivace, 6/8 tarantella and movement separation; Zanetti documents the later cyclic melodic recall, also supported by a provisional form relation. That later return is not placed at this boundary.

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived in our day he would have retained his own style while accepting something of the new at the same time.
quote.source: Autobiography, explaining the Classical Symphony of 1917

composer.background:
Prokofiev grew up on the Sontsovka estate in Ukraine, where his father managed the agricultural business and his mother played Beethoven and Chopin at the piano. He remembered hearing sonatas from another room after being put to bed. The keyboard was therefore familiar before the concert hall: his mother wrote down his first pieces, and a visit to Moscow opera performances in 1900 prompted the nine-year-old to compose The Giant for performance at home. Sergei Taneyev subsequently recommended professional instruction. Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka, teaching composition and helping the boy turn his accumulating pieces into larger forms.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing manuscripts of his compositions. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Anatoly Lyadov harmony and counterpoint, Nikolai Tcherepnin conducting, and Anna Esipova piano. Tcherepnin’s attention to Haydn and Mozart mattered as much as the harmonic experiments Prokofiev pursued outside class. Nikolai Myaskovsky, an older fellow student, became a lifelong correspondent and a critic whose objections he took seriously. Their correspondence continued to test decisions about form and orchestration long after the Conservatory.
composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: A pianist who made the keyboard strike like percussion, and a theatre composer whose longest melodies keep their footing through abrupt changes of key.
